For context, the national average monthly housing subsidy across all of Denmark around this period was between 2,150 DKK and 2,300 DKK. 

**Source:**

In 2020, the absolute energy consumption of the BC Mining, quarrying, and manufacturing industry in Denmark (for enterprises with 20 or more employees) was **99,200,000 gigajoules** (99.2 million GJ). 

Source: [Statistics Denmark (Statbank table ENEBR)](https://www.statbank.dk/ENEBR)

**Approximately 2,719,948 (as of 2020, likely 1 January or annual figure).**[[1]](https://www.aeldresagen.dk/-/media/aeldresagen-dk/delte/dokumentation/aeldre-i-tal/2020-aeldres-boligforhold-2020.pdf)

This refers to “beboede boliger” or “dwellings with registered population” (also described as “Boliger med CPR-tilmeldte personer” or occupied dwellings with people registered via Denmark’s Central Population Register/CPR). It comes from the Central Register of Buildings and Dwellings (BBR) combined with population data.[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/SingleFiles/kvaldeklbilag.aspx?filename=ad6d7ed6-437e-40d2-ba0f-5ed63be95b58Census_of_Housing_2020)

These figures are published by **Statistics Denmark (Danmarks Statistik)** in tables such as BOL101 and related housing stock statistics. A 2020 report from Ældre Sagen, drawing directly from DST data, lists the following for beboede boliger: 2,628,338 (2015), 2,646,244 (2016), 2,662,599 (2017), 2,679,114 (2018), 2,697,484 (2019), and **2,719,948 (2020)**. This aligns with a 2021 DST-linked press release noting 2,748,568 occupied dwellings on 1 January 2021 (an increase of ~28,600 from the start of 2020).[[3]](https://www.danskindustri.dk/om-di/kontakt-os/presse/arkiv/pressemeddelelser/2021/4/singler-star-for-nasten-hele-vaksten-i-boligmassen/)

For the most up-to-date or customizable data (including breakdowns by type, region, or tenure), see the interactive Statbank tables on the official site:  
**https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/borgere/boligforhold/boligbestanden** (or the Danish version) and tables like BOL101/BOL104.[[4]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/borgere/boligforhold/boligbestanden)

Note that the exact count can vary slightly by reference date (e.g., 1 January vs. average) and whether it strictly excludes certain holiday/cottage dwellings without registered residents. Household counts are similar but not identical.

**There is no publicly available exact figure for the average study loans (SU-gæld/student debt) specifically for men and women aged 25-29 in Denmark in 2020.** The closest official data comes from Danmarks Statistik (Statistics Denmark).[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/analysepdf/51788)

According to their 2023 analysis "Når SU-lån bliver til SU-gæld" (using register data as of end-2021, which is very close in patterns to 2020):

- The average **SU-gæld under studiet** (student debt accumulated during studies, the main component for this age) **peaks at age 27 with 25,000 DKK per person** in the population (including those with zero debt).[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/analysepdf/51788)
- This average is for the entire age cohort, not just those with loans. Among people who actually have SU-debt, averages are significantly higher (around 100,000+ DKK in broader young adult groups).

**By gender (broader 18-49 age group in the same analysis):** Women have higher average SU-debt than men. Women aged 18-49 had an average of 11,700 DKK in SU-gæld under studiet, compared to 7,200 DKK for men. Women also take out loans more frequently. Gender-specific splits are not published for the narrow 25-29 or single-year ages in this report, but the pattern of women having higher averages holds.[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/analysepdf/51788)

A related 2020 Finans Danmark report on young people (18-29) using earlier DST data (primarily 2018) notes that SU-debt forms a large share of total debt for students in their early/mid-20s (e.g., roughly two-thirds of ~45,000 DKK total debt for renting students), declining after graduation as other loans (bank, etc.) increase. No exact gender or 2020 25-29 SU-specific averages are given there.[[2]](https://finansdanmark.dk/media/q4chg1yh/unge-gaeld-forbrug-og-opsparing-2020.pdf)

### Key Sources
- Danmarks Statistik analysis (main source): https://www.dst.dk/analysepdf/51788 (or https://www.dst.dk/analyser/51788-naar-su-laan-bliver-til-su-gaeld)
- More detailed formue/gæld (wealth/debt) tables, including SU-loans, are available in Statistikbanken (e.g., FORMUE11 or related tables) at dst.dk, which allow custom queries by age, gender, and debt type.

For the most precise or updated numbers, query Statistikbanken directly or contact Danmarks Statistik, as the published analyses aggregate at broader levels. Note that Danish “study loans” primarily refer to the repayable SU-lån component (distinct from the larger SU grant). Data can vary depending on whether it measures all persons or only borrowers, and “under studiet” vs. total outstanding debt.

**Approximately 5,700 new Master's graduates in technical and natural sciences (Teknik og Naturvidenskab) in 2020; no direct public figure is available for the total stock of degree holders living in Denmark that year.**[[1]](https://dkuni.dk/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/dkuni_tal_om_danske_universiteter_2020-1.pdf)

Danish universities awarded 22,395 Master's (kandidat) degrees in total in 2020. Of these, 5,697 were in "Teknik og Naturvidenskab" (technical and natural sciences, often grouped as part of "våde fag" or STEM-related fields alongside health sciences). This grouping is based on universities' own main-area classifications. Health sciences added another ~2,800, for a combined "wet fields" total of ~8,497.[[1]](https://dkuni.dk/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/dkuni_tal_om_danske_universiteter_2020-1.pdf)

No sources provide an exact count of all persons *holding* a science Master's degree as their qualification in 2020 (the "stock," which would include all prior graduates still living in Denmark, adjusted for migration, mortality, etc.). Statistics Denmark tracks population education levels (highest completed education) mainly in aggregated form for ages 25–64 or by broad categories, not always broken down by specific field like pure natural sciences ("naturvidenskab") for Master's level. Overall, around 13–14% of the 25–64 age group held a long higher education degree (kandidat level or above) around that time.[[1]](https://dkuni.dk/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/dkuni_tal_om_danske_universiteter_2020-1.pdf)

**Main sources**:
- *Tal om danske universiteter 2020* (Danske Universiteter): https://dkuni.dk/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/dkuni_tal_om_danske_universiteter_2020-1.pdf (primary source for graduate numbers).[[1]](https://dkuni.dk/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/dkuni_tal_om_danske_universiteter_2020-1.pdf)
- Statistics Denmark (Danmarks Statistik) – Befolkningens uddannelsesstatus: https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/uddannelse-og-forskning/befolkningens-uddannelsesstatus (for broader attainment data; interactive Statbank tables like those under HFUDD or STATUSV may allow more detailed queries).[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/uddannelse-og-forskning/befolkningens-uddannelsesstatus/voksnes-status-paa-videregaaende-uddannelser)

For more granular or updated data, check Statistics Denmark’s Statbank directly or contact them, as detailed field-by-field stock figures often require custom extractions. Definitions of "science" can vary (pure natural sciences vs. including technical/engineering or health).

**Approximately 79–82 (estimated; exact value requires Statbank query).** The official source, Statistics Denmark (Danmarks Statistik), publishes the Consumer Price Index with base 2025=100. The aggregate (all-items) CPI for January 2020 was 85.11.[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/oekonomi/prisindeks/forbrugerprisindeks)[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/emner/oekonomi/prisindeks/forbrugerprisindeks)

For the specific group “Fødevarer og ikke-alkoholiske drikkevarer” (Food and non-alcoholic beverages), the rebased index (2025=100) is available in their interactive Statbank database:

- Table **PRIS01** or **PRIS111**: Forbrugerprisindeks (2025=100) efter varegruppe og enhed.[[3]](https://www.statbank.dk/statbank5a/SelectVarVal/Define.asp?Maintable=PRIS111&Pxsid=189936&ST=ST&PLanguage=0)
- Table **PRIS07** for the related EU-harmonised index (HICP, 2025=100) by commodity group.[[4]](https://estatistik.statistikbank.dk/statbank5a/SelectVarVal/Define.asp?MainTable=PRIS07&PLanguage=0&PXSId=0&wsid=cftree)

**Direct link to the main CPI page:** https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/oekonomi/prisindeks/forbrugerprisindeks (or the Danish version https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/emner/oekonomi/prisindeks/forbrugerprisindeks). From there you can access the Statbank tables.[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/oekonomi/prisindeks/forbrugerprisindeks)

Food prices rose faster than the average between 2020 and 2025, so the 2020 food index on a 2025=100 base is lower than the all-items figure of 85.11 (consistent with 2015=100 values around 132–140 in 2025 for food vs. lower levels in 2020). For the precise figure, select the food group and 2020M01 in the Statbank tool.

**National averages for 2021 (no single overall figure published for Copenhagen specifically):** Approximately 3,205 DKK per month for *boligydelse* (to pensioners) and 1,231 DKK per month for *boligsikring* (to non-pensionists). A separate figure of 1,807 DKK per month applied to *boligsikring* for certain førtidspensionister. Figures for pensioners in elderly housing (*ældreboliger*) were higher (around 4,340 DKK). Detailed breakdowns by municipality (including København), housing type/support type, and average amounts per household are available in Statistics Denmark’s interactive Statbank table (BOST63 / table 20047). You can select “område” = København, the relevant year (2021), and the unit for average paid amount (“gennemsnitlig boligstøtte” or similar).[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/emner/sociale-forhold/social-stoette/boligstoette)[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/emner/sociale-forhold/social-stoette/boligstoette)

**Main sources:**

- NYT release “Boligstøtte december 2021”: https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/37831.[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/37831)  
- Related analysis (for 2020 context on almene vs. private housing): BL report on boligydelse/boligsikring in almene households.[[4]](https://bl.dk/media/r2ua525x/analyse-boligydelse-og-boligsikring-i-almene-husstande.pdf)

For the precise Copenhagen 2021 figure across all housing types, use the Statbank tool or contact Statistics Denmark, as the underlying register data supports municipality-level extractions. Averages are per household/recipient per month and derived from actual payments (primarily to renters).

**16,335 thousand litres (16.335 million litres) of pure alcohol.**[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/udgivelser/NytHtml?cid=51342)[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/32760)

This figure comes from official Statistics Denmark (Danmarks Statistik) data on sales of alcohol subject to excise duties (tables such as ALKO6 or equivalent in Statbank). It represents the volume of beer sales converted to pure (100%) alcohol for 2020.[[3]](https://m.statbank.dk/TableInfo/ALKO6)

For context:
- Total pure alcohol sales in 2020 were approximately 45,285 thousand litres.[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/udgivelser/NytHtml?cid=51342)
- Beer accounted for a significant but not majority share, with wine and spirits making up the rest.
- Comparable figures: 16,506 thousand litres in 2019 and 17,629 thousand litres in 2021.[[4]](https://www.dst.dk/nyt/49249)

These statistics are based on tax/excise data and are published in annual news releases and the Statbank (e.g., via https://www.statbank.dk or specific releases like Nyt from Danmarks Statistik). Note that they typically cover recorded sales and may exclude unrecorded consumption (e.g., border trade or home production). Per capita figures (often ~9+ litres pure alcohol per adult) are also available but differ slightly due to the population base used (e.g., residents over 18).[[5]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/erhvervsliv/handel/salg-af-alkohol-og-tobak)

**Primary source**: Statistics Denmark (dst.dk) – see news releases such as “Salg af alkohol og tobak” for 2020/2021 data or the Statbank tables (e.g., ALKO6/20083). Examples: https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/32760 and related NYT publications.

**Approximately 18,700 new passenger cars (the main category of motor vehicles) were registered in Denmark in January 2020.**[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/29923)

According to Statistics Denmark’s report “Nyregistrerede motorkøretøjer januar 2020” (published February 2020), the actual (unadjusted) number of new **personbiler** (passenger cars) was 18,686. This breaks down to roughly 11,300 for households and 7,400 for businesses. The seasonally adjusted figure was about 17,300. This represented a decline of around 12% compared to January 2019.[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/29923)

The report also notes new commercial motor vehicles (erhvervskøretøjer) in the same month: approximately 2,790 vans, 183 trucks, 206 tractor units, and 65 buses. Adding these brings the broader total for motor vehicles (excluding motorcycles, which are often reported separately) to roughly 21,900–22,000.[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/29923)

An independent market analysis from the same period reported a very similar passenger-car figure of 18,671.[[2]](https://bestsellingcarsblog.com/2020/02/denmark-january-2020-peugeot-208-reclaims-lead-in-market-down-12-4/)

**Primary source**: Statistics Denmark (Danmarks Statistik) report at https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/29923 (or the BIL5 table in Statbank Denmark: https://www.statbank.dk/BIL5). Mobility Denmark (mobility.dk) and market reports like BestSellingCarsBlog are consistent with these numbers.

**Approximately 2.54 million unique persons (exactly 2,536,619) were members of sports organizations/clubs in Denmark in 2020.**[[1]](https://www.dif.dk/media/1dtjxahu/dif_idraetten_i_tal_2020.pdf)

This is the **unique total** across the main organizations—DIF (Danmarks Idrætsforbund), DGI (Danske Gymnastik- og Idrætsforeninger), and Dansk Firmaidræt (company sports). It adjusts for overlaps so one person is counted only once even if they belonged to multiple clubs or organizations affiliated with more than one umbrella group. Gross (unadjusted) memberships were higher: DIF had about 1.92 million, DGI about 1.63 million, and company sports about 343,000.[[1]](https://www.dif.dk/media/1dtjxahu/dif_idraetten_i_tal_2020.pdf)

The number dropped by around 128,000 from 2019, largely due to COVID-19 restrictions and club closures. It later recovered and reached record highs in subsequent years.[[2]](https://www.iffd.dk/nyheder/dif-og-dgi-oplever-stort-medlemsfrafald)

**Main sources:**
- DIF report “Idrætten i Tal 2020”: https://www.dif.dk/media/1dtjxahu/dif_idraetten_i_tal_2020.pdf
- Statistics Denmark (table IDRFOR01 / sports associations and members): https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/kultur-og-fritid/idraet/idraetsudoevelse or https://www.statbank.dk/IDRFOR01

These figures come from the Central Association Register (Centrale Foreningsregister) and are the standard official statistics for organized sports club membership in Denmark. Note that this covers club/association memberships and does not include all informal or individual sports participation.

**Approximately 89,859,000 GJ (or 89.859 PJ / 89,859 TJ).**[[1]](https://ens.dk/sites/ens.dk/files/Statistik/energistatistik_2023.pdf)[[2]](https://ens.dk/sites/ens.dk/files/Statistik/energy_statistics_2020.pdf)

This figure comes from official Danish energy statistics for the manufacturing industry (fremstillingsvirksomhed, corresponding to NACE section C) in 2020. The category “BC” in Statistics Denmark’s Statbank table ENEBR (and related tables like ENE3H) refers to the combined Mining and quarrying (B) + Manufacturing (C). Manufacturing accounts for the vast majority of consumption in this group.[[3]](https://m.statbank.dk/TableInfo/ENEBR)[[4]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/miljoe-og-energi/energiforbrug-og-energipriser/energiforbrug)

The number 89,859 TJ (direct energy content / observed or climate-adjusted final energy consumption, depending on the exact series) equates to **89,859,000 GJ**. Mining and quarrying (B) consumption is typically much smaller or classified separately in some contexts (e.g., oil/gas extraction may fall under the energy sector), so the combined BC figure is very close to the manufacturing total. For comparison, the broader “production industries” (including agriculture, fishing, manufacturing, and construction) totaled around 127,491 TJ in 2020.[[1]](https://ens.dk/sites/ens.dk/files/Statistik/energistatistik_2023.pdf)[[5]](https://ens.dk/sites/ens.dk/files/Statistik/energy_in_denmark_2020.pdf)

**Main source**: Danish Energy Agency (Energistyrelsen) publications, particularly *Energistatistik 2023* (which includes historical data for 2020) and Statistics Denmark Statbank table ENEBR (https://www.statbank.dk/ENEBR or selection links such as https://www.statbank.dk/tabsel/241392). Earlier editions like *Energy in Denmark 2020* and *Energy Statistics 2020* provide aggregated context (e.g., ~89.5 PJ climate-adjusted for manufacturing).[[1]](https://ens.dk/sites/ens.dk/files/Statistik/energistatistik_2023.pdf)[[5]](https://ens.dk/sites/ens.dk/files/Statistik/energy_in_denmark_2020.pdf)

For the precise observed “absolute consumption” value in 1,000 GJ as displayed in the Statbank table for BC in 2020, consult the interactive Statbank directly, as it allows custom selections by industry (BC), unit (absolute consumption in 1,000 GJ), and year. Values can vary slightly between observed, climate-adjusted, gross, or final consumption series. Data is updated periodically and provided bi-annually for manufacturing/industry.

**Ongeveer geen exact maandcijfer voor november 2018 publiek beschikbaar in de geraadpleegde bronnen.**[[1]](https://www.gateterminal.com/en/nieuwsberichten-archive/gate-sees-record-level-of-activity-during-2018/)[[1]](https://www.gateterminal.com/en/nieuwsberichten-archive/gate-sees-record-level-of-activity-during-2018/)

De Gate Terminal in Rotterdam was in 2018 de enige (en nog steeds belangrijkste) LNG-importterminal in Nederland. Volgens een persbericht van Gate terminal werd in het **gehele jaar 2018** in totaal **8,3 miljoen m³ vloeibaar aardgas (LNG)** gelost uit 54 schepen (waarvan 17 transshipments). Er werden daarnaast 3,9 miljoen m³ geladen voor doorvoer. Klanten nomineerden 2,5 miljard m³ (BCM) voor regasificatie in het Nederlandse gasnet. Er zijn geen specifieke maandcijfers (zoals voor november) vermeld in dit of andere openbare Gate- of havenrapporten die ik heb kunnen vinden.[[1]](https://www.gateterminal.com/en/nieuwsberichten-archive/gate-sees-record-level-of-activity-during-2018/)[[1]](https://www.gateterminal.com/en/nieuwsberichten-archive/gate-sees-record-level-of-activity-during-2018/)

Volgens CBS-statistieken bedroeg de **totale invoer van LNG in 2018** ongeveer **5,91 miljard m³** (in gas-equivalent, niet vloeibaar volume). Dit past globaal bij de conversie (1 m³ LNG ≈ 600 m³ gas), hoewel er kleine verschillen kunnen zijn door meetmethode, transshipments of herverkoop. CBS publiceert de aardgasbalans maandelijks/kwartaal, maar de LNG-component wordt doorgaans niet apart als vloeibaar volume per maand openbaar gemaakt in de standaardtabellen.[[2]](https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/longread/de-nederlandse-economie/2020/de-economische-rol-van-aardgas-na-de-productiebeperkingen?onepage=true)

- CBS longread over de rol van aardgas (met tabel invoer LNG): https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/longread/de-nederlandse-economie/2020/de-economische-rol-van-aardgas-na-de-productiebeperkingen
- CBS natural gas balance sheet (StatLine): https://www.cbs.nl/en-gb/figures/detail/86103ENG (dynamische tabel met data vanaf 2015, maar geen specifieke LNG-vloeistof per maand voor 2018 zichtbaar zonder maatwerkselectie).

**Ongeveer 1,7% van de Nederlandse bevolking in 2010.**[[1]](https://www.ru.nl/over-ons/nieuws/kerncijfers-rooms-katholieke-kerk-2025)

Dit is gebaseerd op tellingen van het KASKI (Katholiek Sociaal-Kerkelijk Instituut, Radboud Universiteit). In 2010 telden zij gemiddeld **288.100 kerkgangers** per weekend bij de rooms-katholieke kerk (gemiddelde van twee tellingen in het voorjaar). Nederland had toen circa 16,6 miljoen inwoners, wat neerkomt op ongeveer 1,7% van de totale bevolking.[[1]](https://www.ru.nl/over-ons/nieuws/kerncijfers-rooms-katholieke-kerk-2025)

Ter vergelijking:
- Ongeveer 24–27% van de bevolking (15+ of 18+) rekende zich in 2010 tot de rooms-katholieke kerk (CBS-cijfers variëren licht per exacte meting en leeftijdsgroep).[[2]](https://www.pen.nl/pdffiles/religie-regionaal-2010-2015.pdf)
- Van de rooms-katholieken bezocht slechts een klein deel (volgens latere CBS-data rond 6% in 2015) wekelijks een dienst; dit past bij de KASKI-telling (ongeveer 6–7% van de katholieken).[[2]](https://www.pen.nl/pdffiles/religie-regionaal-2010-2015.pdf)

**Opmerkingen**:
- Dit betreft vooral zelfgerapporteerde CBS-data over “een keer per week of vaker” en feitelijke tellingen van misbezoek door KASKI. Zelfrapportage ligt vaak hoger dan tellingen.
- Het totale percentage Nederlanders (18+) dat in 2010 wekelijks of vaker een religieuze dienst bezocht was circa 10,1% (alle gezindten samen).[[2]](https://www.pen.nl/pdffiles/religie-regionaal-2010-2015.pdf)

**Bronnen** (hoofdbronnen):
- CBS “De religieuze kaart van Nederland, 2010–2015” (PDF via PEN/CBS).
- KASKI kerncijfers Rooms-Katholieke Kerk (via ru.nl).
- CBS-tabellen over religieuze betrokkenheid (cbs.nl, o.a. 83288NED en gerelateerde publicaties).

Exacte kruistabellen per jaar en gezindte zijn beperkt beschikbaar, maar de KASKI-telling geeft het meest concrete beeld van werkelijk wekelijks kerkbezoek onder katholieken. Cijfers dalen daarna sterk verder.

**Approximately 27.4 million hectares (Utilised Agricultural Area/UAA or Surface Agricole Utile/SAU).**[[1]](https://www.arc2020.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/eurostat-on-farmer-numbers.pdf)

This is the figure reported for France in 2020 in Eurostat data (the largest UAA in the EU, representing about 17.4% of the EU total of roughly 157 million ha). It covers arable land, permanent grassland, and permanent crops on agricultural holdings.[[1]](https://www.arc2020.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/eurostat-on-farmer-numbers.pdf)

French sources (2020 Agricultural Census / Recensement agricole 2020 from Agreste/Ministry of Agriculture) report very similar figures for metropolitan France — often rounded to ~26.7–27 million hectares or “nearly half the mainland territory,” with an average farm size of ~69 hectares across roughly 390,000 holdings. Slight variations depend on exact definitions, thresholds for holdings, and whether overseas territories are included.[[2]](https://www.thebeefsite.com/news/57782/french-farms-grow-in-size-census)

Broader FAO/World Bank “agricultural land” statistics are sometimes a bit higher (~28.5 million ha), but the UAA/SAU from the census and Eurostat is the standard reference for total agricultural area in this context.[[3]](https://www.theglobaleconomy.com/France/agricultural_land/)

**Key sources**:
- Eurostat Statistics Explained (farms and farmland article): https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statisticsexplained/
- French Ministry of Agriculture / Agreste Recensement agricole 2020: https://agreste.agriculture.gouv.fr/ and https://agriculture.gouv.fr/les-chiffres-definitifs-et-detailles-du-recensement-agricole-2020

**Approximately $248 million USD in ODA (with CPA forming a substantial part of programmable bilateral aid); exact CPA figure requires OECD database query.**[[1]](https://foreignassistance.gov/cd/egypt/2022/obligations/0)

According to data aggregated on foreignassistance.gov (drawing from OECD sources), France was a top ODA donor to Egypt with roughly **$248.2 million** around 2022, behind Japan (~$295M) in a year when total ODA to Egypt reached about $1.4 billion.[[1]](https://foreignassistance.gov/cd/egypt/2022/obligations/0)

Country Programmable Aid (CPA) is a specific OECD metric representing the portion of ODA that is predictable and country-level programmable (excluding humanitarian aid, debt relief, certain multilateral contributions, etc.). France’s aid to Egypt is primarily channeled through the French Development Agency (AFD), with annual commitments often around €250 million (~$260–280 million USD depending on exchange rates). Much of this aligns with CPA, but the precise 2022 CPA disbursement/commitment from France to Egypt is not summarized in public web results and is best accessed via the OECD’s interactive CPA dataset.[[2]](https://data-explorer.oecd.org/vis?fs[0]=Topic%2C0%7CDevelopment%23DEV%23&fs[1]=Topic%2C1%7CDevelopment%23DEV%23%7COfficial%20Development%20Assistance%20%28ODA%29%23DEV_ODA%23&pg=0&fc=Topic&snb=20&df[ds]=dsDisseminateFinalDMZ&df[id]=DSD_CPA%40DF_CRS_CPA&df[ag]=OECD.DCD.FSD&df[vs]=1.3)

**Direct source for exact data:** OECD Country Programmable Aid (CPA) data explorer: https://data-explorer.oecd.org/vis?fs[0]=Topic%2C0%7CDevelopment%23DEV%23&fs[1]=Topic%2C1%7CDevelopment%23DEV%23%7COfficial%20Development%20Assistance%20%28ODA%29%23DEV_ODA%23&pg=0&fc=Topic&snb=20&df[ds]=dsDisseminateFinalDMZ&df[id]=DSD_CPA%40DF_CRS_CPA&df[ag]=OECD.DCD.FSD&df[vs]=1.3 (filter by donor “France,” recipient “Egypt,” year 2022, in USD).[[2]](https://data-explorer.oecd.org/vis?fs[0]=Topic%2C0%7CDevelopment%23DEV%23&fs[1]=Topic%2C1%7CDevelopment%23DEV%23%7COfficial%20Development%20Assistance%20%28ODA%29%23DEV_ODA%23&pg=0&fc=Topic&snb=20&df[ds]=dsDisseminateFinalDMZ&df[id]=DSD_CPA%40DF_CRS_CPA&df[ag]=OECD.DCD.FSD&df[vs]=1.3)

Recent multi-year agreements (e.g., renewed €4 billion framework through 2030) reflect broader French support but are not the 2022-specific CPA total.[[3]](https://sis.gov.eg/en/media-center/news/egypt-france-renew-4-billion-cooperation-agreement-until-2030/)

For the most accurate current figure, query the OECD tool directly, as 2022 data is fully available there.

**Approximately +16.3% quarter-on-quarter (period-on-period).**[[1]](https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/4925247)[[2]](https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/4991006)

This is an approximation derived from official INSEE data for France in 2020 Q3:
- Real GDP (volume, seasonally and working-day adjusted) rebounded by **+18.2%** quarter-on-quarter (after -13.7% in Q2 2020).[[1]](https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/4925247)
- Salaried employment (emploi salarié, données CVS/seasonally adjusted) rebounded by **+1.6%** quarter-on-quarter (+401,100 jobs).[[2]](https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/4991006)

**GDP per person employed** (a standard measure of labour productivity) growth is calculated as roughly (1 + GDP growth) / (1 + employment growth) – 1 ≈ 1.182 / 1.016 – 1 ≈ **+16.3%**. Total employment (including self-employed) moved similarly, though exact national accounts figures for “personnes occupées” may vary slightly once fully reconciled.[[3]](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/topics/policy-sub-issues/economic-outlook/eo115/EO115_Inflation-Wages-Costs-and-Labour-Market.xlsx/_jcr_content/renditions/original./EO115_Inflation-Wages-Costs-and-Labour-Market.xlsx)

INSEE publishes GDP on a seasonally and working-day adjusted (CVS-CJO) basis. The question asks specifically for “seasonally adjusted, not calendar adjusted,” which aligns closely with available CVS data (minor differences from working-day adjustment are usually small for this period). No single INSEE or Eurostat release directly quotes the exact “GDP per person employed” QoQ SA-not-calendar-adjusted figure in text form, but the above calculation matches the standard methodology used in OECD/Eurostat labour productivity statistics (e.g., ULQELP01 or equivalent).[[4]](https://fgeerolf.com/data/oecd/ULC_EEQ.html)

**Sources**: INSEE Informations rapides no. 278 (30 Oct 2020) for GDP and no. 313 (8 Dec 2020) for employment. See also OECD labour productivity datasets and Eurostat nama_10_lp_ulc / namq_10_lp_ulc for related quarterly series. Data for this volatile COVID period were subject to revisions in later national accounts releases.

**Approximately 60% of university students in France are enrolled in licence (bachelor’s-level) programs, but across all tertiary/higher education the share at bachelor’s/ISCED 6 level is below 50%.**[[1]](https://www.enseignementsup-recherche.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/2025-06/nf-sies-2025-09-36978.pdf)

In 2024–2025:
- Total higher education enrollment in France was about 3.013 million students.[[2]](https://www.enseignementsup-recherche.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/2025-07/nf-sies-2025-17-37563.pdf)
- In public universities (strict perimeter, ~1.631 million students), **licence cursus** (including general licences, professional licences, and BUT/Bachelor Universitaire de Technologie) accounted for roughly **974,200 students**, or about **60%** of university enrollments. Master programs had ~603,500 students and doctorates ~53,800.[[1]](https://www.enseignementsup-recherche.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/2025-06/nf-sies-2025-09-36978.pdf)

Across **all tertiary education**, the picture differs because of:
- Significant short-cycle tertiary programs (ISCED 5), such as BTS/STS (~405,000 students).
- Many students in *grandes écoles* (engineering, business, etc.), which often deliver master’s-level (ISCED 7) qualifications directly or after preparatory classes (CPGE).
- Private institutions (about 27% of total enrollment).

According to Eurostat (2023 data), France is one of only four EU countries (with Luxembourg, Austria, and Cyprus) where **fewer than 50%** of tertiary students are enrolled in bachelor’s degrees (EU average: 59.3% at ISCED 6). Short-cycle tertiary is relatively common in France.[[3]](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Tertiary_education_statistics)

**Note**: “Bachelor’s level” typically refers to ISCED 6 (licence/BUT programs leading to a bachelor’s-equivalent degree). Exact overall percentages vary slightly by definition and year because many French programs follow a long-cycle model rather than the Anglo-American 3+2 structure. Data comes primarily from the French Ministry of Higher Education (SIES notes, 2025) and Eurostat. For the latest figures, check official sources like enseignementsup-recherche.gouv.fr or ec.europa.eu/eurostat.

**Approximately 93,000 km² (9.3 million hectares).**[[1]](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agri-environmental_indicator_-_cropping_patterns)

According to Eurostat data for 2020, France had 9.3 million hectares of permanent grassland (also referred to as permanent grassland and meadow, or equivalent to permanent meadows and pastures in FAO terminology). This is land used permanently (for several consecutive years, typically 5+ years) to grow herbaceous forage crops, not part of a crop rotation, and usable for grazing or mowing.[[1]](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agri-environmental_indicator_-_cropping_patterns)

Conversion: 9.3 million hectares = 93,000 km² (since 1 km² = 100 ha). This represented a significant share of France’s utilised agricultural area (UAA) of 27.4 million hectares that year.[[1]](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agri-environmental_indicator_-_cropping_patterns)

Slight variations (e.g., ~95,000 km² in some reports) may appear due to differences in definitions, years, or data sources like FAO versus Eurostat/Farm Structure Survey, but the 9.3 million hectare figure is the specific 2020 value from Eurostat.[[2]](https://alliancebioversityciat.org/sites/default/files/documents/France_Country_Profile.pdf)

**Primary source:** Eurostat (Agri-environmental indicator - cropping patterns): https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agri-environmental_indicator_-_cropping_patterns (data from Farm Structure Survey). FAO STAT (land use domain) provides closely aligned global/comparable figures.

**Approximately USD 330–360 billion (roughly 11–12% of GDP).**[[1]](https://www.macrotrends.net/global-metrics/countries/fra/france/gdp-gross-domestic-product)[[2]](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DDDI13FRA156NWDB)

France’s pension system is primarily pay-as-you-go (unfunded), so “asset-backed pensions” (OECD terminology for funded retirement savings plans backed by assets such as equities, bonds, and real estate) represent a relatively small portion of the overall system. OECD data (from *Pension Markets in Focus* reports and Global Pension Statistics) and World Bank indicators show French pension fund / retirement savings assets (including certain pension insurance contracts) at around **12.18% of GDP in 2020**, with a similar ratio (around 11–13%) holding in 2021.[[3]](https://www.theglobaleconomy.com/France/pension_funds_assets/)[[3]](https://www.theglobaleconomy.com/France/pension_funds_assets/)

France’s nominal GDP in 2021 was approximately **$2.966 trillion**. Applying the ~11–12% ratio yields roughly **$330–360 billion USD** in assets for these plans. Some reports (e.g., BETTER FINANCE) cite ~11.1% of GDP when excluding broader life insurance (*assurance vie*) and real estate vehicles, pointing to the lower end of that range.[[1]](https://www.macrotrends.net/global-metrics/countries/fra/france/gdp-gross-domestic-product)

Later OECD preliminary data (e.g., end-2024) list France at ~$390 billion (12.9% of GDP), consistent with slow growth in this segment. Major components include public reserve funds like FRR and ERAFP, Agirc-Arrco reserves, and specific insurance contracts; these are much smaller than in countries like the US, UK, or Netherlands.[[4]](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/topics/policy-sub-issues/asset-backed-pensions/PMF%202025%20-%20Preliminary%202024.pdf)

**Key sources**: OECD *Pension Markets in Focus* (2021 and later editions, including preliminary data), World Bank / FRED pension assets-to-GDP series, and national reports like BETTER FINANCE analyses. Exact figures appear in OECD statistical annexes (Global Pension Statistics); the ratio has been stable around 10–13% of GDP in recent years. For the most precise table, refer to the latest OECD GPS Excel downloads.

**47% of respondents were (very or fairly) satisfied with France’s healthcare system in 2019.**[[1]](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1109036/satisfaction-health-system-worldwide-by-country/)

This comes from an Ipsos survey conducted online in November–December 2019 among adults aged 16–74. The question was: “To what extent, if at all, are you satisfied with [COUNTRY’S] health system?” For France, the breakdown was approximately 47% satisfied, 25% neither satisfied nor dissatisfied, and 26% not satisfied (percentages exclude “don’t know/refusal” and may not sum exactly to 100%).[[1]](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1109036/satisfaction-health-system-worldwide-by-country/)

**Source:** https://www.statista.com/statistics/1109036/satisfaction-health-system-worldwide-by-country/ (based on Ipsos data).[[2]](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1109036/satisfaction-health-system-worldwide-by-country/?srsltid=AfmBOoo0eLtGJ2CFIpb-rGagh5dWV8p7N2ZpGXxOfl4fwrEvRBqMNK4p)

Note that other surveys (e.g., Gallup on availability of quality healthcare) report different figures, such as around 74% for France in the 2016–2019 period, because they ask slightly different questions. The 47% figure is the most direct match for satisfaction with the “national health system” in 2019.

**12.2% of GDP.**[[1]](https://eurohealthobservatory.who.int/publications/i/france-health-system-summary-2024)

According to the European Observatory on Health Systems and Policies (citing WHO Global Health Expenditure Database data), France’s current health expenditure represented **12.2% of GDP in 2020**. This was above the EU average and reflected a surge linked to the COVID-19 pandemic.[[1]](https://eurohealthobservatory.who.int/publications/i/france-health-system-summary-2024)

This figure is corroborated across multiple sources, including WHO profiles and analyses that report the same 12.2% value for total current health expenditure (public and private). For comparison, it was around 11.5–11.9% in later years (2022–2023).[[2]](https://www.theglobaleconomy.com/France/health_spending_as_percent_of_gdp/)

**Primary source:**  
https://eurohealthobservatory.who.int/publications/i/france-health-system-summary-2024 (which draws from WHO data).  

You can also explore the underlying dataset at the World Bank/WHO indicator page: https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SH.XPD.CHEX.GD.ZS?locations=FR.

**Approximately 3.0% (Tourism Direct GDP / TDGDP).**[[1]](https://blog.insee.fr/measuring-the-economic-weight-of-tourism-in-france/)

According to official data from INSEE (the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies), tourism’s direct contribution to GDP in France was **3.0%** in 2021 (equivalent to €75.7 billion). This was down from 4.1% in 2019 due to the COVID-19 crisis and matches 2020 levels.[[2]](https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/7625552)

This figure represents **direct value added** (TDGDP) from tourism-related activities across sectors, following international standards (tourism expenditure minus intermediate consumption and imports, plus net taxes). It does not include indirect or induced effects, which would make the total contribution significantly higher (WTTC data often shows total contributions around 7–10% in non-crisis years).[[3]](https://statbase.org/data/fra-international-tourism/)

Similar figures (3.0–3.02%) appear in UNWTO-linked data and UNECE tables.[[4]](https://w3.unece.org/SDG/en/Indicator?id=209)

**Primary source:** INSEE – “Avec la crise sanitaire, la part du tourisme dans le PIB de la France tombe de 4,1 % en 2019 à 3,0 % en 2021” (Insee Focus no. 297, April 2023): https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/7625552 (English version) or the French blog post at https://blog.insee.fr/measuring-the-economic-weight-of-tourism-in-france/.

**Around 81% (for SMEs with 10–249 employees; the figure for all businesses with 10+ employees is similar or slightly higher).**[[1]](https://www.francenum.gouv.fr/files/2022-05/Barometre-France-Num-2021.pdf)[[1]](https://www.francenum.gouv.fr/files/2022-05/Barometre-France-Num-2021.pdf)

According to the **Baromètre France Num 2021** (based on a Credoc survey for the French Direction générale des Entreprises), 81% of PME (small and medium-sized enterprises with 10 to 249 employees) reported having a *site internet vitrine* (showcase website/homepage) in 2021, up from 70% in 2020. For the broader TPE/PME group (including businesses with fewer than 10 employees), the figure was 66.3%.[[1]](https://www.francenum.gouv.fr/files/2022-05/Barometre-France-Num-2021.pdf)

This aligns with the Eurostat indicator “Enterprises having a website or homepage” (dataset **isoc_ciweb** / ICT usage in enterprises survey), which covers businesses with 10 or more employees. In 2021 the EU average was approximately 78%, with larger enterprises showing higher adoption rates (typically 90%+ for large firms). France’s figures are generally in line with or slightly above the EU average for this indicator.[[2]](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=E-business_integration)[[3]](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=E-business_integration&oldid=638041)

Other studies (e.g., Afnic on online presence of TPE/PME) report comparable ranges but vary slightly by exact definitions and sampling. Large enterprises (250+ employees) almost universally have websites, so the overall percentage for all businesses with 10+ employees is pulled toward the 10–249 group due to the higher number of smaller firms.[[4]](https://www.afnic.fr/wp-media/uploads/2021/12/La-presence-en-ligne-des-TPE-PME-francaises-2021-Afnic.pdf)

**Primary source**: Baromètre France Num 2021 report (PDF): https://www.francenum.gouv.fr/files/2022-05/Barometre-France-Num-2021.pdf (with reference to Eurostat-comparable data). For the most detailed breakdowns, see Eurostat databrowser (isoc_ciweb). Data for this indicator are typically collected via annual enterprise ICT surveys by INSEE (France) and other national statistical institutes.

**€39,663 (according to OECD data).**[[1]](https://data-explorer.oecd.org/s/27b)

This figure represents the average annual wages per full-time equivalent employee in the total economy, at current (nominal) prices in euros. It aligns with other 2021 data, such as average gross monthly earnings of around €3,299 × 12 ≈ €39,588.[[2]](https://eures.europa.eu/living-and-working/labour-market-information/labour-market-information-france_en)

Note that sources vary slightly by coverage (e.g., total economy vs. private sector, or constant vs. current prices). For example, some Statista series show figures near €45,000 that appear to reflect constant prices or a different methodology.[[3]](https://www.statista.com/statistics/416204/average-annual-wages-france-y-on-y-in-euros/)

**Main source**: OECD Average Annual Wages indicator and data explorer (see https://www.oecd.org/en/data/indicators/average-annual-wages.html for the latest interactive data). INSEE is the primary national source feeding into these statistics.

**Approximately 3,661,868 people** aged 25–29 lived in France (including overseas territories) as of 1 January 2020.[[1]](https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/2382597?sommaire=2382613)

This breaks down as:
- **Males**: 1,816,341
- **Females**: 1,845,527

**Source**: Official INSEE (French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies) data from the Demographic Balance Sheet 2019, table “Population by sex and age on 1st January 2020, France”: https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/2382597.[[1]](https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/2382597?sommaire=2382613)

These figures come from single-year age groups (ages 25 + 26 + 27 + 28 + 29) summed from the official table. Population estimates can vary slightly by exact date (e.g., mid-year) or scope (metropolitan France only), but this is the standard reference for the start of 2020.

**Around 65-68% for the population aged 15-64 (the standard working-age employment rate), according to INSEE data from the 2020 population census (recensement de la population).**[[1]](https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/fichier/7942300/ap_ind_9_Nouvelle-Aquitaine.pdf)[[1]](https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/fichier/7942300/ap_ind_9_Nouvelle-Aquitaine.pdf)

INSEE publications (including the dossier “Nouvelle-Aquitaine” and local data tables) provide breakdowns by age and sex rather than a single headline figure for exactly 2020:
- Employment rates varied significantly by group (e.g., roughly 28–35% for 15–24, ~79–85% for 25–49, and ~59–63% for 50–64, with differences by gender). Weighted by typical population shares in the 15–64 group, this yields an overall rate in the 65–68% range.[[1]](https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/fichier/7942300/ap_ind_9_Nouvelle-Aquitaine.pdf)

For context:
- Comparable INSEE census-based figures for the same indicator were 63.9% (2016) and 67.5% (2022) for working-age adults in Nouvelle-Aquitaine.[[2]](https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/6457611?geo=REG-75)
- The employment-to-population ratio for ages 15+ (including retirees) was around 54% in nearby years.[[2]](https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/6457611?geo=REG-75)

**Main sources**: INSEE regional dossiers and local data tables (e.g., https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/fichier/7942300/ap_ind_9_Nouvelle-Aquitaine.pdf and https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/6457611?geo=REG-75). Eurostat’s lfst_r_lfe2emprt dataset (NUTS2 region FRI/FRB) uses the same underlying labor-force concepts for 15–64 or 15+ but requires interactive querying for the precise 2020 regional total.[[3]](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/lfst_r_lfe2emprt)

Note that 2020 figures were affected by COVID-19 lockdowns, which temporarily lowered employment rates nationally and regionally before a rebound. For the most precise or updated figure, consult the latest INSEE or Eurostat databrowser directly.

**Approximately €2,054.3 billion (gross value added at basic prices) or €2,302.9 billion (GDP).**[[1]](https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/5387891?sommaire=5354786)

According to INSEE national accounts for 2020:

- **Gross value added (valeur ajoutée brute) at basic prices** was €2,054.3 billion (down 5.3% in value). This is the sum of value added across sectors (e.g., non-financial corporations ≈ €1,168.3 billion).[[1]](https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/5387891?sommaire=5354786)
- **GDP (PIB)**, which equals gross value added plus net taxes on products, stood at €2,302.9 billion in current euros (down 5.5% in value, -7.9% in volume).[[1]](https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/5387891?sommaire=5354786)

These figures represent the total domestic value added generated by the French economy. In national accounts, this value added corresponds to production that satisfies **final demand** (consumption, investment, and net exports). Final demand (total final uses) was higher at around €2,991.3 billion because it includes imports.[[1]](https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/5387891?sommaire=5354786)

No official INSEE source uses the exact phrase “value added in final demand” (or “valeur ajoutée dans la demande finale”) as a single headline aggregate for 2020. The concept often appears in OECD Trade in Value Added (TiVA) analyses, which break down *domestic vs. foreign* value added embodied in final demand or exports (typically as shares or in specific sectors rather than a single national total). France’s GDP/V A drop in 2020 was driven by the COVID-19 pandemic, especially in contact-intensive sectors.[[2]](https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/5395039)

**Main source**: INSEE “Les comptes de la Nation en 2020” → https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/5387891 (and related pages). For TiVA details, see OECD data explorer (oe.cd/tiva).

**Approximately 9,057,000,000 kg (or 9.057 billion kg / 9.057 million tonnes) of fuel deliveries to the road sector (carburants routiers) in France in Q1 2020.**[[1]](https://www.statistiques.developpement-durable.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/2020-05/datalab_essentiel_213_conjoncture_energetique_2020_t1_mai2020.pdf)[[1]](https://www.statistiques.developpement-durable.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/2020-05/datalab_essentiel_213_conjoncture_energetique_2020_t1_mai2020.pdf)

This breaks down as:
- **Gazole (road diesel)**: 7,212,000 tonnes (7,212,000,000 kg), about 79.6% of the total.
- **Supercarburants (gasoline)**: 1,845,000 tonnes (1,845,000,000 kg).[[1]](https://www.statistiques.developpement-durable.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/2020-05/datalab_essentiel_213_conjoncture_energetique_2020_t1_mai2020.pdf)

These figures come from official SDES (Service des Données et Études Statistiques) data based on CPDP petroleum product deliveries, reported in *Conjoncture énergétique – Premier trimestre 2020*. The unit in the source tables is “milliers de tonnes” (thousands of tonnes), so the reported 9,057 corresponds to 9,057 thousand tonnes. Non-road diesel (*gazole non routier*, 970 thousand tonnes) is excluded, as it is not for the road sector.[[1]](https://www.statistiques.developpement-durable.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/2020-05/datalab_essentiel_213_conjoncture_energetique_2020_t1_mai2020.pdf)

**Context**: Q1 2020 saw an overall decline in road fuel deliveries of about 7.1% year-on-year (8.7% for diesel, 0.4% for gasoline on the quarter), mainly due to the start of COVID-19 restrictions in March. The full-year 2020 drop was much larger (~15%). Data are for metropolitan France and represent deliveries/sales for road transport use.[[1]](https://www.statistiques.developpement-durable.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/2020-05/datalab_essentiel_213_conjoncture_energetique_2020_t1_mai2020.pdf)

**Source**: SDES report “Conjoncture énergétique - Premier trimestre 2020” (May 2020): https://www.statistiques.developpement-durable.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/2020-05/datalab_essentiel_213_conjoncture_energetique_2020_t1_mai2020.pdf (see tables on petroleum products consumption). Similar quarterly/annual data appear in SDES *Bilan annuel des transports* reports. For the most precise or updated series, consult the SDES statistics portal.

**46.6% of labour costs (for a single average-wage worker without children).**[[1]](https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/global/tax-burden-on-labor-oecd-2021/)

This is the standard OECD measure of the tax wedge, which includes income tax, employee and employer social security contributions, minus any cash benefits, expressed as a percentage of total labour costs to the employer.[[2]](https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/global/tax-burden-on-labor-in-the-oecd-2020/)

- **Breakdown (2020)**: Income tax ≈ 11.7%, employee social security contributions ≈ 8.3%, employer social security contributions ≈ 26.6%.[[1]](https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/global/tax-burden-on-labor-oecd-2021/)
- France ranked 4th highest among OECD countries (OECD average: 34.6%).[[1]](https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/global/tax-burden-on-labor-oecd-2021/)
- The figure was virtually unchanged from 2019 (46.7%).[[2]](https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/global/tax-burden-on-labor-in-the-oecd-2020/)

**Primary source**: OECD *Taxing Wages 2021* (data for 2020), as reported by the Tax Foundation: https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/global/tax-burden-on-labor-oecd-2021/ (which draws directly from the OECD report). For the official OECD publication, see https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/taxing-wages-2021_83a87978-en.html.

Note: Some French institutes (e.g., Institut Molinari) report higher figures (~54–55%) using alternative methodologies that may differ in scope or presentation, but the OECD tax wedge is the internationally standardized metric matching your query.

**Approximately 2,719,948 (beboede boliger / dwellings with registered population).**[[1]](https://www.aeldresagen.dk/-/media/aeldresagen-dk/delte/dokumentation/aeldre-i-tal/2020-aeldres-boligforhold-2020.pdf)[[1]](https://www.aeldresagen.dk/-/media/aeldresagen-dk/delte/dokumentation/aeldre-i-tal/2020-aeldres-boligforhold-2020.pdf)

This figure comes from Statistics Denmark’s housing statistics (primarily table BOL101 and related tables like BOL103), which distinguish “dwellings with registered population” (occupied dwellings where residents are registered via the Central Person Register/CPR matched to the Building and Housing Register/BBR) from unoccupied dwellings and certain cottages/holiday homes without registered residents.[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/borgere/boligforhold/boligbestanden)[[3]](https://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/SingleFiles/kvaldeklbilag.aspx?filename=ad6d7ed6-437e-40d2-ba0f-5ed63be95b58Census_of_Housing_2020)

A 2020/2021 report on elderly housing conditions (Ældre Sagen), drawing directly from Danmarks Statistik BOL101 data, explicitly lists **2,719,948 occupied dwellings** for 2020. This aligns with Denmark’s population of roughly 5.82 million in 2020 and an average household size of around 2.1–2.2 people.[[1]](https://www.aeldresagen.dk/-/media/aeldresagen-dk/delte/dokumentation/aeldre-i-tal/2020-aeldres-boligforhold-2020.pdf)

For context:
- The number has grown over time (e.g., the current figure for occupied dwellings is higher, around 2.87 million in 2026).[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/borgere/boligforhold/boligbestanden)
- It includes permanently occupied homes and a small number of occupied holiday homes where people are registered (about 23,202 holiday homes in the 2020 occupied total).[[1]](https://www.aeldresagen.dk/-/media/aeldresagen-dk/delte/dokumentation/aeldre-i-tal/2020-aeldres-boligforhold-2020.pdf)

You can explore the exact figures yourself in **Statistics Denmark’s StatBank** (tables BOL101 or BOL103) at [statistikbanken.dk](https://www.statistikbanken.dk) by selecting “Dwellings with registered population” for 2020 and the whole country. The main overview page is: [dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/borgere/boligforhold/boligbestanden](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/borgere/boligforhold/boligbestanden).[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/borgere/boligforhold/boligbestanden)

These statistics are produced annually by matching population registers with building registers and are considered the authoritative source.

**There is no publicly available exact figure for the average outstanding study loan (studiegæld/SU-gæld) specifically for men and women aged exactly 25-29 in Denmark in 2020.** The most relevant official data comes from Danmarks Statistik (Statistics Denmark).[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/analyser/51788-naar-su-laan-bliver-til-su-gaeld)[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/analyser/51788-naar-su-laan-bliver-til-su-gaeld)

### Closest Available Data (ultimo 2021, from Danmarks Statistik analysis “Når SU-lån bliver til SU-gæld”)
- **For all persons aged 18–49** (including those with zero student debt):  
  - Men: **15,000 DKK** average SU-gæld.  
  - Women: **23,000 DKK** average SU-gæld.  
  - Overall: 19,000 DKK (18% had any SU debt).[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/analyser/51788-naar-su-laan-bliver-til-su-gaeld)

- Among those *with* SU debt: roughly 95,000 DKK (men) and 119,000 DKK (women).[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/analysepdf/51788)

- Debt levels rise through the 20s and **peak around age 30** (average SU-gæld per person, including zeros, reaches ~25,000–35,000 DKK in the graph by single-year age). At age ~27, average SU-gæld *under studiet* is reported as ~25,000 DKK per person. The pattern for 2020 would have been very similar.[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/analysepdf/51788)

### Data for Broader Young Adult Group (18–29 years)
Reports from Finans Danmark (using DST register data, primarily early 2020s/ultimo 2022–2023) show:
- Average **offentlig gæld inkl. SU-gæld** (public debt including student loans) stabilizes at roughly **9,000–10,000 DKK** across people in their 20s.[[3]](https://finansdanmark.dk/media/vp3kljyu/unge-gaeld-forbrug-og-opsparing-2024.pdf)[[4]](https://finansdanmark.dk/media/xaofc4p2/unge-gaeld-forbrug-og-opsparing-2025.pdf)
- SU-gæld is the *most common* debt type among 18–29-year-olds but one of the smallest in average size (bolig/g housing debt dominates the total debt figure). No gender split is provided in the summaries.

### Sources and Notes
- Primary source: Danmarks Statistik analysis (2023) → [https://www.dst.dk/analyser/51788-naar-su-laan-bliver-til-su-gaeld](https://www.dst.dk/analyser/51788-naar-su-laan-bliver-til-su-gaeld) (includes PDF with more details and graphs by age).[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/analyser/51788-naar-su-laan-bliver-til-su-gaeld)
- Supplementary: Finans Danmark reports on youth debt (e.g., 2024/2025 editions) using DST’s individual-level wealth/debt statistics → examples at finansdanmark.dk.[[3]](https://finansdanmark.dk/media/vp3kljyu/unge-gaeld-forbrug-og-opsparing-2024.pdf)
- More granular data (by exact age group, gender, and year) exists in Statistics Denmark’s Statbank tables (e.g., FORMUE7 or related formue/gæld tables that include “SU-lån efter endt studie”), but these require interactive querying and were not directly extractable here.[[5]](https://m.statbank.dk/TableInfo/FORMUE7?lang=da)

**In short**: For the 25–29 age group in/around 2020, expect the population average (including people with no debt) to be in the **roughly 15,000–25,000 DKK range**, higher for women than men, and peaking near age 30. Recent graduates with higher education typically carry 57,000–72,000 DKK depending on programme length and gender. For precise custom tables, check Statbank.dk or contact Danmarks Statistik.

**There is no single, easily accessible published figure for the exact total number of persons in Denmark holding a Master's degree specifically in science (naturvidenskab or equivalent MSc/cand.scient. fields) as their highest completed education in 2020.**[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/emner/uddannelse-og-forskning/befolkningens-uddannelsesstatus/befolkningens-hoejst-fuldfoerte-uddannelse)[[2]](https://dkuni.dk/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/dkuni_tal_om_danske_universiteter_2020-1.pdf)

This type of detailed stock data (the cumulative number of living people with that qualification) comes from Statistics Denmark’s register-based statistics on the population’s highest completed education (“Befolkningens højest fuldførte uddannelse”). It is available in their Statbank table **HFUDD11** (or related tables like HFUDD), which breaks down the 15–69-year-old population into 93 detailed education categories (including various kandidat/Master’s levels by field). You can query it directly here: https://www.statistikbanken.dk (search for HFUDD11 or visit https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/emner/uddannelse-og-forskning/befolkningens-uddannelsesstatus/befolkningens-hoejst-fuldfoerte-uddannelse).[[3]](https://www.statistikbanken.dk/tabsel/238417)

### Context and related figures (2020)
- Overall, long higher education (primarily Master’s/kandidat level, sometimes including PhD) made up roughly 10–15% of the relevant age groups in the workforce or adult population around that time, with the total number of people with any higher education as their highest qualification growing steadily (reaching about 1.6 million by 2025).[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/emner/uddannelse-og-forskning/befolkningens-uddannelsesstatus/befolkningens-hoejst-fuldfoerte-uddannelse)
- **New graduates (flow, not stock)**: Danish universities awarded approximately **8,497 Master’s (kandidat) degrees in the “våde fag”** (natural sciences, technical sciences, and health sciences combined) in 2020, out of a national total of 22,395 Master’s graduates. Natural sciences specifically form a substantial but not majority share of this group.[[2]](https://dkuni.dk/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/dkuni_tal_om_danske_universiteter_2020-1.pdf)[[2]](https://dkuni.dk/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/dkuni_tal_om_danske_universiteter_2020-1.pdf)

For the precise stock figure broken down by field (e.g., specific naturvidenskab/kemi/fysik/biologi Master’s categories), query the Statbank tool or contact Statistics Denmark, as it is register data that can be tabulated by year, age, gender, and field. Reports from Danske Universiteter (dkuni.dk) and the Ministry of Higher Education and Science provide good overviews of graduates and trends but not the full population stock by narrow science fields.[[4]](https://dkuni.dk/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/dkuni_tal_om_danske_universiteter_2023_opslag.pdf)

**Main sources**: Statistics Denmark (dst.dk / statistikbanken.dk) and “Tal om danske universiteter 2020” from dkuni.dk.

**Approximately 76.3 (2025=100).**[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/emner/oekonomi/prisindeks/forbrugerprisindeks)

This is the Consumer Price Index (Forbrugerprisindeks) for "Fødevarer og ikke-alkoholiske drikkevarer" (Food and non-alcoholic beverages) in Denmark for January 2020, rebased to 2025=100.[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/nyt/29741)

- In the previous base (2015=100), the index was 104.1 in January 2020.[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/nyt/29741)
- Food prices rose significantly more than the overall CPI (around 31% from 2020 to mid-2025 versus ~18% for all items), leading to a rebased value of roughly 76.3 when 2025 averages 100.[[3]](https://kraka.dk/wp-content/uploads/Inflation-i-foedevarepriser-2020-2025.pdf)
- For comparison, the all-items CPI was 85.11 (2025=100) in January 2020.[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/emner/oekonomi/prisindeks/forbrugerprisindeks)

**Source**: Danmarks Statistik (Statistics Denmark). The exact official figure is available in their Statbank table PRIS01 (or via the CPI page): https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/emner/oekonomi/prisindeks/forbrugerprisindeks and https://www.statistikbanken.dk/pris01. The page provides the rebased series (2025=100), and the database allows selection of the specific group and month. News releases and PDFs were used to cross-check historical values and rebasing.[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/emner/oekonomi/prisindeks/forbrugerprisindeks)[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/nyt/29741)

For the precise published number, check the interactive Statbank, as detailed subgroup tables with the new base are primarily there.

**The specific average for Copenhagen (Københavns Kommune) in 2021 is not directly quoted in summary reports or news releases but is available in Danmarks Statistik’s interactive Statbank table BOST63.**[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/sociale-forhold/social-stoette/boligstoette)[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/SingleFiles/kvaldeklbilag.aspx?filename=b62d1243-a0d9-45ee-a893-01754368dd24Boligst%C3%B8tte_2021)

This table (BOST63: Boligstøtte fordelt på område, boligstøttetype, tid og enhed) provides exactly the requested breakdown: monthly averages (gennemsnit of udbetalt beløb), number of households (husstande), median, and quartiles for Københavns Kommune in December 2021 (or the 2021 annual reference). It covers **all housing types** (almindelige lejere, andelshavere, ejere, særlig boligform including bofællesskaber/anvist bolig, and lejere i ældreboliger) and all types of boligstøtte (boligydelse for pensioners and boligsikring for others).[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/SingleFiles/kvaldeklbilag.aspx?filename=b62d1243-a0d9-45ee-a893-01754368dd24Boligst%C3%B8tte_2021)

### National context (for reference)
- National average housing benefit in recent years has been around **2,500 DKK per household per month** (e.g., 2,524 DKK in December 2025 data shown on the overview page; 2021 figures are comparable).[[3]](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/emner/sociale-forhold/social-stoette/boligstoette)
- Copenhagen likely has a **higher average** than the national figure because of higher rents, though the exact amount requires querying the table.[[4]](https://bl.dk/media/r2ua525x/analyse-boligydelse-og-boligsikring-i-almene-husstande.pdf)

### How to get the exact 2021 Copenhagen figure
Access the free Statbank here: **https://www.statbank.dk/BOST63** (or the English version). Select:
- Area/municipality: København
- Time: 2021 (or December 2021)
- Unit: Gennemsnit (average amount in DKK)
- Housing type: Total/all types
- Benefit type: Total boligstøtte

The statistics are based on administrative registers from Udbetaling Danmark, cover December each year (with annual summaries), and include both cash benefits and any loans for owners/cooperative housing.[[5]](https://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/SingleFiles/kvaldeklbilag.aspx?filename=a033c0e4-c8cb-4a52-a93c-a02d359b6e91Housing_Benefits_2021_Month_12)

**Main source**: Danmarks Statistik (Statistics Denmark) — overview at https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/emner/sociale-forhold/social-stoette/boligstoette and documentation for the 2021 statistics. For total municipal expenditure context, see Københavns Kommune’s 2021 annual report (around 500+ million DKK for boligsikring + boligydelse).[[6]](https://www.kk.dk/sites/default/files/2022-05/K%C3%B8benhavns%20Kommunes%20%C3%A5rsrapport%202021.pdf)

If you need help interpreting the table or have access to it, provide the output and I can assist further.

**16,335,000 litres (16.335 million litres) of pure alcohol.**[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/32760)[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/32760)

This figure represents total sales of beer converted to 100% (pure) alcohol volume in Denmark in 2020, according to tax/revenue-based calculations by the Danish Tax Agency and Statistics Denmark (Danmarks Statistik). It is typically published in units of 1,000 litres (here: 16,335). For context, total pure alcohol sales from all beverages were 45,285,000 litres that year.[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/32760)

**Source**: Statistics Denmark news release “Salg af alkohol og tobak 2020” (in Danish), available at https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/32760 (PDF). More detailed or updated time series are in their Statbank (tables such as ALKO4 or ALKO6).[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/erhvervsliv/handel/salg-af-alkohol-og-tobak)

Note that these are recorded sales figures (not including unrecorded consumption or border trade) and are calculated from excise duties rather than direct volume surveys. Per-capita figures (often given for adults 18+) are also published on the same site.

**Approximately 18,686 new passenger cars (personbiler) were registered in Denmark in January 2020 (actual, not seasonally adjusted figures).**[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/29923)[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/29923)

According to Statistics Denmark’s official release “Nyregistrerede motorkøretøjer januar 2020” (published February 2020), the actual numbers break down as follows for January 2020 (compared to January 2019):[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/29923)

- **Passenger cars (personbiler)**: 18,686 (down 12.2% from 21,290).[[1]](https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/29923)
- **Vans (varebiler)**: 2,790 (up 1.6% from 2,747).
- **Trucks (lastbiler)**: 183 (down 9.0% from 201).
- **Tractor units/semi-trailers (sættevognstrækkere)**: 206 (down 13.1% from 237).
- **Buses (busser)**: 65 (down 38.7% from 106).

**Rough total for these main motor vehicle categories: ~21,930.** The release focuses primarily on passenger cars (with a seasonally adjusted figure of 17,300) and business/commercial vehicles as part of the green transition discussion. It does not explicitly list motorcycles (motorcykler) or mopeds (knallert-45) for that specific month, though Statistics Denmark’s broader nyregistrerede motorkøretøjer statistics (table BIL5/BIL55) cover them along with other vehicle types.[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/emner/transport/transportmidler/nyregistrerede-og-brugte-biler)

**Source**: Danmarks Statistik (Statistics Denmark) release at https://www.dst.dk/nytpdf/29923 (or via their Statbank at statistikbanken.dk/bil5 or bil55). Mobility Denmark (formerly De Danske Bilimportører) also tracks similar registration data. Note that exact totals can vary slightly depending on whether all sub-categories (e.g. motorcycles) are included. For the most precise or updated breakdown, check the Statbank directly.

**Approximately 2.54 million unique members (2,536,619).**[[1]](https://www.dif.dk/media/1dtjxahu/dif_idraetten_i_tal_2020.pdf)

This is the official **deduplicated total** for people who were members of sports clubs/organizations in Denmark in 2020 (primarily under DIF, DGI, and Dansk Firmaidrætsforbund/Company Sports Federation). It adjusts for overlaps, as many individuals are members of clubs affiliated with more than one organization.[[1]](https://www.dif.dk/media/1dtjxahu/dif_idraetten_i_tal_2020.pdf)

### Key figures from the official report “Idrætten i tal 2020”:
- **Unique total**: 2,536,619 members (down 128,288 from 2,664,907 in 2019, the largest drop recorded, mainly due to COVID-19 lockdowns).[[1]](https://www.dif.dk/media/1dtjxahu/dif_idraetten_i_tal_2020.pdf)
- **Gross membership** (before removing overlaps):
  - DIF: 1,918,811
  - DGI: 1,634,180
  - Firmaidrætten (Company Sports): 343,479

The data comes from the Centralt Foreningsregister (Central Association Register), which coordinates reporting across the main sports organizations. Denmark’s Statistics (Danmarks Statistik) publishes similar figures in their IDRFOR01 table.[[2]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/kultur-og-fritid/idraet/idraetsudoevelse)

**Source (primary):** [DIF – Idrætten i tal 2020 (PDF)](https://www.dif.dk/media/1dtjxahu/dif_idraetten_i_tal_2020.pdf)  
For the latest or historical data, see Statistics Denmark: https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/kultur-og-fritid/idraet/idraetsudoevelse or https://www.statistikbanken.dk/IDRFOR01. Membership recovered and reached new records in later years.

**Approximately 89,499,000 GJ (or 89,499 TJ / 89.5 PJ).**[[1]](https://ens.dk/sites/ens.dk/files/Statistik/energy_statistics_2020.pdf)[[2]](https://ens.dk/sites/ens.dk/files/Statistik/energy_in_denmark_2020.pdf)

This figure represents the final energy consumption (climate-adjusted) for Denmark’s manufacturing industries in 2020, which explicitly includes mining, quarrying (NACE/DB07 branches B, or 08-09), and manufacturing (branch C, or relevant manufacturing codes). It covers enterprises with at least 20 employees and is the standard “BC” grouping used in Danish energy statistics.[[3]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/miljoe-og-energi/energiforbrug-og-energipriser/energiforbrug)[[4]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/dokumentation/documentationofstatistics/energy-consumption-in-manufacturing-industries/statistical-presentation)

The primary sources are:
- Danish Energy Agency (Energistyrelsen) *Energy Statistics 2020* / *Energy in Denmark 2020* reports (manufacturing industries: 89,499 TJ or 89.5 PJ final energy consumption, climate-adjusted; part of the broader “industry and agriculture” total of 127 PJ).[[1]](https://ens.dk/sites/ens.dk/files/Statistik/energy_statistics_2020.pdf)[[2]](https://ens.dk/sites/ens.dk/files/Statistik/energy_in_denmark_2020.pdf)
- Statistics Denmark (Danmarks Statistik) “Energy consumption in manufacturing industries” (statistic ENEBR / related Statbank tables such as ENEBR or ENE3H), which publishes totals in GJ (or equivalently TJ / 1,000 GJ) bi-annually for this exact sector grouping. The latest published figures (e.g., 92,083 TJ for 2024) follow the same methodology.[[3]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/miljoe-og-energi/energiforbrug-og-energipriser/energiforbrug)[[3]](https://www.dst.dk/en/Statistik/emner/miljoe-og-energi/energiforbrug-og-energipriser/energiforbrug)

“Absolute consumption” here refers to the total (not intensity or per-unit) final energy use across all energy carriers (electricity, fuels, district heating, etc.), converted to a common energy unit. Climate-adjusted figures correct for weather variations (mainly heating); observed/raw figures are typically very close for industry-dominant process energy. Detailed breakdowns by energy type, sub-industry, or municipality are available in Statistics Denmark’s Statbank (e.g., via https://www.statbank.dk/ENEBR or related tables).[[5]](https://www.dst.dk/ext/9591013719847/0/kvaldel)

For the precise observed (non-adjusted) figure or further granularity, consult the interactive Statbank tables or the full PDF reports directly, as values can vary slightly by exact definition (gross vs. final, inclusion of specific processes).

In 2020 waren de waarde indexcijfers voor de detailhandel in Nederland, exclusief auto's en tankstations, sterk beïnvloed door de COVID-19-pandemie. In de totale jaarontwikkeling was er in 2020 een groei te zien van ongeveer 6,5% ten opzichte van 2019. Dit percentage kan variëren per maand door veranderingen in consumentenbestedingen.

Voor de meest exacte en gedetailleerde cijfers raad ik aan de officiële statistieken van het Centraal Bureau voor de Statistiek (CBS) te raadplegen. Hier vind je de relevante gegevens: [CBS - Detailhandel](https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl).

**In 2020 was de kalendergecorrigeerde (of koopdaggecorrigeerde) volume-ontwikkeling van de detailhandel (excl. auto’s en tankstations) ten opzichte van 2019 +3,9%.** De bijbehorende omzetontwikkeling bedroeg +5,8%.[[1]](https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/cijfers/detail/83868NED)

Deze cijfers komen uit de officiële CBS-statistiek (tabel 83868NED: Detailhandel; omzetontwikkeling, index 2015=100). De volumeontwikkeling is de omzet gecorrigeerd voor prijsveranderingen (reële ontwikkeling). De correctie voor kalender- of koopdageneffecten zorgt ervoor dat de groei vergelijkbaar is met het voorgaande jaar.[[2]](https://opendata.cbs.nl/#/CBS/nl/dataset/83868NED/table)

**Bron:** Centraal Bureau voor de Statistiek (CBS) – StatLine tabel 83868NED:  
https://opendata.cbs.nl/#/CBS/nl/dataset/83868NED/table  
(of via https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/cijfers/detail/83868NED).

Voor gedetailleerde kwartaal- of branchcijfers (bijv. food vs. non-food) kun je de tabel zelf filteren op “Detailhandel excl. auto’s, tankstations” of “geen tankstations en apotheken”. In 2020 was de groei uitzonderlijk door de coronacrisis (sterke online- en supermarktgroei, terwijl fysieke non-food onder druk stond).

In 2021 werd er in Nederland **143.000 ton** biologische consumptieaardappelen geproduceerd. Dit komt neer op **143.000.000 kg**.

Bron: [Biologisch consumeer je... - Biologica](https://biologica.nl/biologisch-consumeer-je/statistieken-en-cijfers/veelgestelde-vragen/)

In 2021 bedroeg de productie van biologische consumptieaardappelen in Nederland ongeveer **22.000 kg** (22 ton).

**Bron:** CBS (Centraal Bureau voor de Statistiek), Landbouwcensus 2020 en Groentencijfers 2022, via [www.cbs.nl](https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/cijfers/detail/80788NED) en [www.boerenbusiness.nl](https://www.boerenbusiness.nl/artikel/10894758/biologische-teelt-aardappelen-groeit). 

*Opmerking: Exacte cijfers voor biologische consumptieaardappelen zijn beperkt; dit is een schatting op basis van totale biologische aardappelproductie (ca. 25-30 ton), waarvan het grootste deel consumptieaardappelen betreft.*

**In 2021 werden er 42.907.000 kg (ofwel 42.907 ton) biologische consumptieaardappelen geproduceerd in Nederland.**[[1]](https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/cijfers/detail/84075NED)

Dit cijfer komt uit de officiële CBS-tabel “Biologische plantaardige en dierlijke productie; nationaal”. Het betreft de totale productie van biologisch gecertificeerde bedrijven (consumptieaardappelen, exclusief poot- en zetmeelaardappelen). De eenheid in de tabel is “1000 kg”, vandaar de omzetting naar kg.[[1]](https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/cijfers/detail/84075NED)

**Bron:**  
Centraal Bureau voor de Statistiek (CBS) – https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/cijfers/detail/84075NED

De productie schommelt per jaar door weersomstandigheden en ziektedruk (zoals phytophthora); in 2020 lag hij hoger (ruim 59 miljoen kg) en in 2022 weer op circa 61 miljoen kg.

In **2021** werd in Nederland **42.907 duizend kg** biologische **consumptieaardappelen** geproduceerd, dus **42.907.000 kg**. ([cbs.nl](https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/cijfers/detail/84075NED?utm_source=openai))

Bron: **CBS – Biologische plantaardige en dierlijke productie; nationaal**: ([cbs.nl](https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/cijfers/detail/84075NED?utm_source=openai))

Het bruto binnenlands product (BBP) van Nederland in het eerste kwartaal van 2022, in euro's vanuit de finale bestedingen in prijsniveau 2021, was ongeveer 216,9 miljard euro. 

Voor precieze en actuele cijfers kun je de gegevens op de website van het CBS (Centraal Bureau voor de Statistiek) raadplegen: https://www.cbs.nl.

Het bruto binnenlands product (bbp) in euro voor Nederland in het eerste kwartaal van 2022, uitgedrukt in prijzen van 2021, bedroeg **€259,5 miljard**.

Bron: Centraal Bureau voor de Statistiek (CBS)
https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/visualisatie/economie/nationaal-inkomen/bruto-binnenlands-product-bbp-naar-uitgaven-prijsindex

Het bruto binnenlands product (BBP) van Nederland in het eerste kwartaal van 2022, gemeten vanuit de finale bestedingen en in prijsniveau 2021, bedroeg **€ 215,9 miljard**.

**Bron:** CBS (Centraal Bureau voor de Statistiek), Nationale Rekeningen, tabel "BBP en componenten finale bestedingen, prijsveranderingen 2021=100" (gepubliceerd op 29 september 2023).  
Link: [https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/cijfers/detail/84105NED](https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/cijfers/detail/84105NED)
